9110: An interlude is a short break, pause, or interval that occurs in the middle of something larger — separating two parts of an experience, a performance, or a period of time. The word always implies something that sits between two things, interrupting the flow temporarily before it continues. This is its most essential quality: an interlude is never at the beginning, never at the end — it always lives in the middle.

When people use "interlude" in ordinary conversation, they mean a brief period that is noticeably different from the time surrounding it. If it has been raining all day and the sun comes out for an hour before the clouds return, that sunny hour is an interlude. If you've been working hard for months and you take a short trip before diving back into work, that trip is an interlude. If two people are having a long, tense argument but share a moment of laughter in the middle before the tension resumes, that laughter is an interlude.

Notice the pattern: an interlude contrasts with what surrounds it. It provides a kind of variety, relief, or change — before things return to how they were.
In theater — the original and most specific use

The most historically precise use of the word is in drama. An interlude was a short, usually light or humorous performance inserted between the acts of a longer, more serious play. Picture yourself watching a heavy, intense tragedy. Between Act 2 and Act 3, a short comic skit is performed — partly to give the audience's emotions a rest, partly to fill time while the stage is being rearranged. That short skit is called an interlude.

This theatrical meaning captures everything the word stands for: something brief, different in character, placed deliberately in the middle of something larger.

In music, an interlude is a short passage played between the main sections of a larger piece. In a song, it might appear between two verses — a brief instrumental section that gives the listener variety before the vocals return. In an opera, it is an orchestral piece performed between scenes or acts, often while the scenery is being changed. The purpose is the same as in theater: a deliberate pause that separates two bigger parts.
The tone and feeling of the word

"Interlude" has a slightly poetic, elevated quality to it. When someone uses this word, they're suggesting that the break was noticeable — that it felt meaningfully different from what came before and after. Saying "we enjoyed a brief interlude of peace" feels more reflective than saying "things were quiet for a bit." The word signals that you noticed the contrast, that the pause had a certain value or beauty to it, even if only for a short while.

This is why writers and speakers reach for "interlude" when they want to give weight to a temporary moment — it implies the moment stood apart.

An interlude is not a permanent change. It's always followed by a return to — or continuation of — the larger thing it interrupted. It is not the beginning of something new and it is not an ending. If a vacation turns into a permanent lifestyle change, it was never really an interlude. If a pause becomes the main event, it ceases to be an interlude. The word specifically means temporary and in-between.

"There was a brief interlude of quiet before the noise of the city returned." (everyday)

"The composer wrote a gentle interlude between the two dramatic movements." (music)

"Their walk in the park was a welcome interlude from an exhausting week." (figurative)

"A short comic interlude was performed between the acts of the tragedy." (theater)

An interlude is a temporary break or interval — brief, distinct in character, and always placed in the middle of something larger. It separates two parts of a bigger whole and typically contrasts with the mood or activity around it. Whether in theater, music, or everyday life, the word captures the idea of a meaningful pause — a breath of something different — before the main experience continues.
9111:
Intermarriage is a noun that refers to the act or practice of marriage between people who belong to different groups — or, in a separate but related sense, marriage that happens within a group, among its own members. It is most commonly used to talk about marriage that crosses the boundaries of race, ethnicity, religion, nationality, caste, or tribe.

The word carries the idea of a boundary — a line that separates one group of people from another — and a marriage that either crosses that line or stays strictly within it.

Meaning 1: Marriage Between Different Groups (the most common use today)

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in books, news, and everyday conversation. Intermarriage here means a marriage where the two people come from different racial, ethnic, religious, or cultural backgrounds.

Think of it this way: if a person from a Hindu family marries a person from a Muslim family, that is a religious intermarriage. If a Black person marries a white person, that is a racial intermarriage. If a Korean person marries a Mexican person, that is an ethnic or national intermarriage.

The key idea is crossing a group boundary. Society — at different times and places — has defined certain groups (by race, religion, caste, tribe, etc.), and intermarriage is what happens when someone marries outside the group they belong to.

Meaning 2: Marriage Within a Group (the older, more technical use)

This meaning sounds like the opposite, and it can be confusing at first — but it makes sense once you understand it. In historical and anthropological writing, "intermarriage" sometimes refers to the practice of people within the same community marrying among themselves, repeatedly over generations.

For example: "European royal families practiced intermarriage for centuries" — this means that kings, queens, and nobles kept marrying other royals and nobles, not ordinary people. They married within their circle, keeping power and bloodlines inside the group.

So in this sense, "inter-" means among (within a group), not between (across groups).
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context is your best guide. When the sentence talks about two different races, religions, or ethnicities coming together, it's Meaning 1. When the sentence talks about a closed circle of people repeatedly marrying each other, it's Meaning 2. In modern, everyday English, Meaning 1 is far more common.
What Intermarriage Refers to as a Noun

As a noun, "intermarriage" can refer to:

A single act — one specific marriage that crosses (or stays within) a group boundary. "Their intermarriage surprised both families."

A practice or phenomenon — the broader pattern of such marriages happening across a community or society over time. "Intermarriage between the two communities has increased over the decades." Here, it's not talking about one marriage, but the general trend.
The Social Weight of the Word

"Intermarriage" is not just a dry, technical word — it carries real social and historical weight. Throughout history, many societies had strict laws or customs against intermarriage, especially across racial or caste lines. For example, interracial marriage was illegal in parts of the United States until 1967. In India's caste system, marrying outside one's caste was — and in some places still is — considered deeply taboo.

Today, in most contexts, "intermarriage" is used as a neutral, descriptive word — it simply describes a fact about who married whom. But depending on the culture, community, or time period being discussed, the word can carry a sense of controversy, progress, tradition, or social change.

• "The rate of intermarriage between different ethnic groups has risen sharply over the past 50 years." (Meaning 1 — crossing group lines)
  • "The isolated mountain village practiced intermarriage for generations, leading to a closely knit but genetically homogeneous population." (Meaning 2 — marrying within the group)
  • "Their intermarriage was seen as a bold act in a society that discouraged mixing between castes." (Meaning 1 — a single act, with social tension)
  • "Scholars debate whether intermarriage is the best indicator of true social integration." (Meaning 1 — used as a concept/phenomenon)
Words That Are Related or Often Confused

Intermarry is simply the verb form. "The two tribes began to intermarry" = they began practicing intermarriage.

Mixed marriage is a common synonym for Meaning 1, especially in the context of race or religion.

Endogamy is a technical/academic term that means the practice of marrying within one's own group (Meaning 2 in formal language).

Exogamy is the opposite — the practice of marrying outside one's group (Meaning 1 in formal language).

Interfaith marriage is a specific type of intermarriage — focused only on religion.

Interracial marriage is a specific type of intermarriage — focused only on race.

Intermarriage is about the relationship between marriage and group identity. It asks: did this marriage stay inside the lines that society drew, or did it cross them? Depending on the context, the word can describe a single union, a social trend, a historical pattern, or a cultural practice — but it always connects the act of marriage to the concept of group boundaries.
9112:
An intermediary is a person or organization that sits between two other parties and helps them connect, communicate, negotiate, or do business — especially when those two parties cannot, will not, or should not deal with each other directly.

Think of it this way: imagine two people standing far apart, unable to reach each other. An intermediary is the bridge between them. They are the "middle person" who makes something happen that otherwise wouldn't.

Whenever you see or use the word intermediary, three things are always true:

  1. There are two separate parties (people, organizations, countries, etc.) on either side.
  2. There is a third party — the intermediary — standing in the middle.
  3. The intermediary's entire job is to facilitate something between those two parties: a deal, a conversation, an exchange, an agreement, or a transaction.

Without the intermediary, the two parties would either struggle to connect or couldn't connect at all.
Real-Life Examples to Make It Concrete

In business: A company in India wants to sell its products to stores in Germany, but it doesn't have contacts there and doesn't know the local market. So it works through a trading company that already has those connections. That trading company is the intermediary — it brings the two sides together and makes the deal possible.

In diplomacy: Two countries are in conflict and refuse to speak to each other directly. A neutral country or an international organization steps in to carry messages, propose solutions, and help them reach peace. That neutral party is acting as an intermediary.

In real estate: When you buy a house, you typically don't negotiate face-to-face with the seller on your own. A real estate agent handles the communication, the offers, and the paperwork between buyer and seller. The agent is the intermediary.

In finance: When ordinary people want to invest their money in the stock market, they don't walk onto a trading floor themselves. They use a broker or a bank. That broker stands between the investor and the market — a financial intermediary.

In personal life: Imagine two friends who had a falling out and are no longer speaking to each other. A mutual friend starts passing messages between them to help them reconcile. That mutual friend is acting as an informal intermediary.
The Key Qualities of an Intermediary

They are always "in between." An intermediary, by definition, is never one of the two main parties. They occupy the middle position. If there is no "middle," there is no intermediary.

They serve a function. An intermediary isn't just a passive observer. They do something — they relay information, negotiate terms, process transactions, build trust, reduce friction, or bridge gaps (in language, culture, geography, knowledge, or power).

They can be neutral or partial. Some intermediaries are completely neutral — like a mediator in a conflict who doesn't take sides. Others are technically in the middle but working in the interest of one party more than the other — like a lawyer negotiating on your behalf. Both are still intermediaries, because they occupy the middle position between parties.

They may or may not have decision-making power. Some intermediaries can finalize deals themselves. Others can only carry messages or proposals back and forth, and the final decision rests with the two main parties. Both types are still intermediaries.

They exist because direct dealing between two parties is sometimes impractical, impossible, inefficient, or even dangerous. Intermediaries solve real problems:

  • Lack of access: One party can't reach the other without a connector.
  • Lack of trust: Two parties don't trust each other, but both trust a common third party.
  • Lack of knowledge or expertise: One party doesn't understand the process, the market, or the rules, so they need a specialist in the middle.
  • Power imbalance: One party is much weaker or smaller, and a representative in the middle can level the playing field.
  • Conflict: Two parties are hostile toward each other and cannot communicate constructively on their own.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are related to intermediary but are not identical:

Mediator — A mediator is a specific type of intermediary. A mediator's job is almost always to resolve a dispute or conflict. All mediators are intermediaries, but not all intermediaries are mediators (because an intermediary doesn't have to be dealing with a conflict — it could just be a business deal).

Middleman — This is a more informal, everyday word that usually refers to a commercial or business context (someone who buys from a producer and sells to a customer). Intermediary is broader, more formal, and can apply to diplomacy, law, finance, and many other fields.

Broker — A broker is a specific kind of intermediary, usually in finance or real estate, who arranges deals between buyers and sellers. The word intermediary is wider in scope.

Agent — An agent typically represents one specific party and acts on their behalf. An intermediary is more neutral in positioning — they serve the connection between both sides, even if they may lean toward one.
One Final Way to Remember It

If you ever forget what intermediary means, remember this image: a relay runner in the middle of a race. The baton (the information, the deal, the message) starts with one person, passes through the intermediary, and reaches the other person at the end. The relay runner in the middle doesn't start or finish the race — but without them, the baton never gets from one side to the other. That runner is the intermediary.
9113:
Interment is the act of placing a dead person's body — or their cremated ashes — into a permanent resting place, such as a grave, tomb, or crypt. In the simplest terms, it is the act of burying the dead.

Think of a funeral. There is usually a service — prayers, speeches, people paying their respects. But at some point, the body actually has to be placed somewhere final. That specific act — the moment and process of laying the remains to rest in their designated place — is the interment.

It's broader than just lowering a coffin into the ground. Interment covers:

  • Burying a body in a grave
  • Placing cremated ashes into the ground (in an urn or urn vault)
  • Placing a body or ashes inside a tomb, crypt, or mausoleum (an above-ground structure)
  • Placing an urn inside a columbarium — a structure with small compartments designed to hold urns

What unites all of these is the idea of placing remains somewhere permanent and designated. That act, in any of these forms, is called interment.
Tone and when you'll see this word

Interment is a formal, dignified word. You'll encounter it in obituaries, funeral announcements, legal documents, and military or religious ceremonies — not in casual everyday conversation. If your friend says "they buried him yesterday," that's the natural, casual way of saying it. But a formal death notice would say "Interment will follow at 2 p.m. at Riverside Cemetery." Both describe the same thing; the register is just different.

• Interment service / interment ceremony — A short, often graveside gathering held at the burial site, usually right after the main funeral service.
  • Private interment — When only close family attends the burial.
  • Military interment — A burial conducted with full military honors.
  • Interment of ashes / cremated remains — When cremated remains are placed in a final resting place.
The most important thing: Don't confuse interment with internment

This is one of the most common and most serious mix-ups in the English language, because these words look almost identical.

  • Interment (one 'n') → burial of the dead
  • Internment (two 'n's) → the act of imprisoning or forcibly confining people, typically by a government, often without a formal trial — usually during wartime or a national emergency

"The interment of veterans at Arlington Cemetery" means they were buried there with honor.

"The internment of Japanese Americans during World War II" means they were forcibly confined in detention camps — not buried. Mixing these two words up would be a serious error in meaning, so always pause and check which one you intend.

• "The interment will take place at 3 p.m. at Greenwood Cemetery, following the church service."
  • "She made arrangements for the interment of her father's ashes in the family plot."
  • "Only immediate family were present for the private interment."
  • "The cemetery has a dedicated section for the interment of military veterans."
  • "After the interment ceremony, guests were invited back to the family home."

• Burial — the everyday, common synonym; what most people say in normal conversation
  • Entombment — specifically placing a body inside a tomb (above-ground structure)
  • Inhumation — a technical term used especially in archaeology and forensic science; it specifically means burial in the ground (as opposed to cremation)
  • Sepulture — a very old, archaic, literary term for burial; rarely used in modern writing

In practice, burial is what you'll say day-to-day, and interment is what you'll write or read in formal contexts. They mean the same thing at their core.
One-line summary to anchor it all:
Interment is the formal word for the act of placing a dead person's remains — whether a body or ashes — into a permanent resting place such as a grave, tomb, or crypt.
9114:
Interminable means seeming to have no end — especially in a way that feels slow, exhausting, or frustrating.

When you describe something as interminable, you mean it goes on and on and on, far beyond what feels reasonable or tolerable. It feels like it will never stop.
The Key Idea: It's About Feeling, Not Just Length

This is the most important thing to understand about this word.

Something interminable isn't necessarily literally endless. It just feels like it is — because it's so drawn out, so slow, or so dull that every minute feels like ten.

Think of the last time you were bored in a meeting, stuck in traffic, or waiting at a doctor's office. Time seemed to crawl. What felt like an hour was only fifteen minutes. That feeling — that dragging, agonizing sense that something refuses to end — is exactly what interminable captures.
The Emotional Weight: It's Always Negative

Interminable is not a neutral word. It always carries a sense of suffering through length. You wouldn't use it to describe something enjoyable. A wonderful movie doesn't feel interminable. A boring lecture does.

So whenever you see or use this word, there's a quiet complaint baked into it — a sense of "when will this finally be over?"

Here are examples that show the word working in real situations:

  • "The flight from New York to Sydney was an interminable journey — eighteen hours of sitting in a cramped seat with nothing to do."
  • "The politician's speech felt interminable; he had been talking for two hours and showed no sign of stopping."
  • "The children sat through what seemed like an interminable wait at the dentist's office."
  • "She stared out the window during the interminable meeting, wishing it would just end."

Notice a pattern: in every sentence, someone is enduring something. They're not enjoying the length — they're suffering through it.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but interminable is special in its own way:

  • "Long" simply describes duration. A long movie. No complaint implied — it might still be great.
  • "Endless" suggests something truly has no finish. It can sometimes be used positively: "endless possibilities." Interminable cannot.
  • "Eternal" often has a grand, even beautiful quality. "Eternal love." Interminable never feels grand — it feels tedious.
  • "Dragging" is similar in feeling but is more informal and casual.

Interminable is the strongest and most sophisticated way to say something felt agonizingly, unbearably long — with no positive spin possible.

Interminable is not a mild word. It's not what you'd say about something that was merely a little long. It's reserved for things that felt truly exhausting in their length — things where the time passing felt like a punishment.

Think of it on a scale:

Long → Very long → Drawn-out → Interminable

Use it when you really want to convey that something tested your patience.

Use interminable when:

  • Something lasted much longer than expected or desired
  • The length made it boring, tedious, or tiring
  • You want to express that it felt like it would never end (even if it eventually did)

Don't use it for:

  • Enjoyable things that happen to be long
  • Casual, everyday contexts where simpler words work fine (it's a formal, slightly literary word)

Interminable = so long and slow that it feels like it will never, ever end — and that's painful.

Hold that image in your mind: a clock ticking in a silent, boring room, with no end in sight. That's interminable.
9115:
Interminably means in a way that seems to have no end, often to the point of being boring, frustrating, or exhausting.

When you say something happens interminably, you mean it goes on and on and on — so long that it feels like it will never stop.

Here is the thing that most people miss: interminably does not mean something is actually endless. It means something feels endless — usually because it is dull, tedious, or unwelcome.

Think about waiting at a doctor's office. You might wait for 45 minutes. That is not truly infinite. But it feels like forever because it is boring and uncomfortable. That is exactly when you would use this word:

"I waited interminably for my name to be called."

The 45 minutes is a real, finite amount of time. But the word captures your experience of it — dragging, crawling, seemingly without end.

This is what makes "interminably" special. It is not just a word about time. It is a word about how time feels to a person.

Interminably almost always carries a negative tone. It signals one or more of these emotions:

  • Boredom — something is going on far too long and is dull.
  • Frustration — you want it to stop, but it keeps going.
  • Impatience — you are waiting for something, but it will not come.
  • Exhaustion — the length of something is wearing you down.

You would almost never use "interminably" to describe something pleasant. You would not say "we laughed interminably" to mean you had a wonderful long laugh — that would sound odd. The word has a built-in sense of suffering through something.
How It Works in a Sentence

"Interminably" is an adverb, which means it modifies (describes) a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. In practice, it almost always modifies a verb.

Modifying a verb:

"The politician spoke interminably."

(He spoke for so long it felt endless.)

"The rain fell interminably."

(The rain kept going and going with no sign of stopping.)

"She waited interminably for a reply."

(The wait felt like it had no end.)

Modifying an adjective:

"It was an interminably long meeting."

(The meeting was so long it felt endless and tedious.)
Words It Loves to Travel With

Certain verbs pair with "interminably" very naturally. You will see these combinations constantly:

  • Drag on interminably — "The film dragged on interminably." (The film felt painfully slow and long.)
  • Go on interminably — "The argument went on interminably." (It kept continuing with no resolution in sight.)
  • Talk interminably — "He talks interminably about football." (He talks about it so much and for so long it is exhausting.)
  • Wait interminably — "We waited interminably for the train." (The wait felt endless.)
  • Stretch on interminably — "The desert stretched on interminably." (It seemed to go on forever with no end in sight.)
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words seem to mean the same thing but do not work in quite the same way.

Endlessly is the closest cousin, but it is more neutral. It can even be used positively:

"She endlessly amazed me." ✅ (Positive — she kept impressing me.)
"She interminably amazed me." ❌ (This sounds wrong — interminably does not suit positive situations.)

Forever is similar but more casual and can be warm or positive:

"I could listen to this music forever." ✅ (Positive, informal.)
"I interminably listened to this music." ❌ (This would imply you were suffering through it.)

Perpetually means something keeps happening continuously as a regular state. It is more neutral:

"She was perpetually cheerful." ✅ (She was always cheerful — neutral or positive observation.)
"She was interminably cheerful." — This would sound slightly sarcastic, implying her cheerfulness was somehow exhausting to be around.

Infinitely is mostly about degree (how much), not time (how long):

"This is infinitely better than the last one." (Far, far better — not really about time at all.)

So interminably is specifically about time that drags on in a tedious or frustrating way. That is its unique lane.
Recognizing the Tone: Objective vs. Subjective

One useful way to think about this word is to notice that it is always told from someone's point of view. It is a subjective word.

  • If you say "the journey lasted eight hours," that is an objective fact.
  • If you say "the journey went on interminably," you are telling us how it felt to someone — exhausting, dreary, seemingly without end.

This is why writers use it so often. It is an efficient way to show a character's inner experience of time without having to spell it out.

"Interminably" is a strong word. It is not mild. It does not mean "for quite a while" or "for a long time." It means the experience of duration was so extended that it was genuinely unpleasant and felt like it would never end. Use it when you want to convey real tedium or real suffering through time — not just a mildly long experience.

What it meansIn a way that seems to have no end; lasting so long it becomes tedious or frustrating
ToneAlmost always negative
Key nuanceAbout how time feels, not how long something actually is
ModifiesVerbs (mostly), sometimes adjectives
StrengthStrong — implies genuine tedium or exhaustion

In short: whenever something drags on so long that you feel like you are trapped inside a moment that will never end — that feeling, and the thing causing it, is described by interminably.
9116:
To intermingle means to mix together freely and thoroughly, especially when two or more different groups, things, or ideas come together and blend among one another — rather than staying separate.

The key idea is mutual mixing. It is not just one thing going into another; both (or all) sides come together and get woven into each other. Think of it like two streams of water flowing into each other — neither stream just "enters" the other. They merge, swirl together, and become one flowing body.

Imagine you have a bowl of red marbles and a bowl of blue marbles. If you pour them both into a large bowl and shake it so the red and blue ones are all mixed up together, scattered among each other — that is intermingling. Neither color stays in its own corner. They are spread throughout each other.

Now apply that same image to people, cultures, ideas, sounds, or anything else — and you have the full power of the word.

Intermingle works in two ways grammatically:

1. Without a direct object (intransitive) — things intermingle on their own:

This is the most common use. The subjects do the mixing themselves — no one is forcing them.

  • The tourists and the locals began to intermingle at the street festival.
  • At the cocktail party, guests from different departments intermingled freely.
  • The smells of garlic, rosemary, and butter intermingled in the kitchen.
  • By the end of the night, the two groups had completely intermingled.

2. With a direct object (transitive) — someone intermingled things:

Here, a person or force actively mixes things together.

  • The chef intermingled the herbs and spices before adding them to the pot.
  • The author skillfully intermingled humor and sadness throughout the novel.
  • The teacher intermingled students from different classes during the project.
The Specific Feeling the Word Carries

This is important: intermingle is not just a fancy word for "mix." It carries a specific shade of meaning that you should understand.

Intermingle suggests:

  • Free movement and mingling among one another — the elements don't just sit next to each other; they move through each other and become scattered among one another.
  • Two or more distinct groups or things — you typically intermingle things that are originally different or separate. There is an awareness that these were once apart, and now they are together.
  • A social or natural process — it often feels organic, relaxed, and natural, not mechanical or forced. People intermingle at a party. Chemicals in a laboratory react or combine. This is an important distinction.
  • Thoroughness — it suggests a fairly complete mixing, not just a light touch. The things are genuinely among each other, not just slightly overlapping.

People and social situations:
This is one of the most common uses. When people from different backgrounds, groups, cultures, or walks of life come together and freely interact with one another — socializing, talking, moving among each other — they intermingle.

  • Delegates from fifty countries intermingled in the conference hall.
  • Rich and poor, young and old — everyone intermingled at the town fair.

Ideas, themes, and feelings:
When different ideas or emotions are woven together in speech, writing, or thought — not kept separately — they intermingle.

  • In her speech, grief and gratitude intermingled beautifully.
  • Throughout the book, themes of love and loss intermingle in complex ways.

Sounds, smells, and sensory things:
When different sensory experiences blend together naturally, they intermingle.

  • The sounds of laughter, music, and clinking glasses intermingled in the hall.
  • The scent of pine and rain intermingled in the mountain air.

Physical things:
When different physical substances or objects are mixed together so that they are scattered among each other.

  • Seeds of different plants intermingled in the old garden.
  • Light and shadow intermingled across the forest floor.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how intermingle is different from similar words is very useful.

Intermingle vs. Mix:
Mix is a broad, everyday word for combining things. Intermingle is more specific — it emphasizes that distinct groups or elements are scattered freely among each other. You mix ingredients in a bowl; people intermingle at a party. Intermingle also tends to feel more formal and descriptive.

Intermingle vs. Mingle:
Mingle has nearly the same meaning and is often used the same way, especially for people socializing. Intermingle simply adds the prefix inter- (meaning "between" or "among"), which gives it a slightly stronger sense of the two or more sides coming together into each other, rather than just being near each other. In practice, the two words are very close, but intermingle feels slightly more thorough and formal.

Intermingle vs. Blend:
Blend often implies that the individual parts become harder to identify — like blending colors to create a new shade. Intermingle usually keeps the individual elements recognizable, even while they are mixed together. People who intermingle at a party are still individuals; they haven't merged into one person.

Intermingle vs. Merge:
Merge suggests two things coming together and becoming one unified whole, often permanently, losing their separate identities (companies merge; lanes of traffic merge). Intermingle keeps the elements distinct even while mixed — they haven't lost themselves into one new thing.
The Register of the Word (Formal or Informal?)

Intermingle sits in the slightly formal to neutral range. You would not typically hear it in very casual everyday conversation — people are more likely to say "mix," "mingle," or "hang out together" in casual speech. However, you would comfortably encounter it in:

  • Written English (books, articles, essays)
  • Journalism and news writing
  • Academic or professional discussion
  • Thoughtful speech or narration

It is never stuffy or overly technical — just a step above casual. A good writer or speaker uses it when they want to convey the precise, visual sense of different things being freely scattered among one another.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Intermingle = when two or more distinct things (people, ideas, sounds, objects, feelings) come together and mix freely among each other, so that they are spread throughout one another rather than staying separate — like two groups of people wandering freely through each other at a gathering, or two melodies weaving in and out of each other in a song.

The word captures togetherness with retained identity — things mix freely, but you can still tell they were once separate. It suggests a natural, organic, thorough mixing, and it is used for both physical things and abstract ones like ideas and emotions.
9117:
An intermission is a planned, temporary break that occurs in the middle of an event, performance, or activity. The event pauses, and then continues again after the break is over. It is not the end of something — it is a breathing space somewhere in the middle.

Think of it like pressing the pause button on a movie, except it is a real-world pause built into a live event on purpose.
The Key Ideas Packed Into This Word

To truly understand "intermission," hold onto three ideas at once:

1. It is planned, not accidental.
An intermission is not an unexpected delay, like a power cut stopping a show. It is a deliberate, scheduled stop that the organizers of an event build into the program from the very beginning. Everyone knows it is coming.

2. It happens in the middle, not at the end.
This is critical. An intermission sits between two parts of an event. The event is not finished — it is only resting. After the intermission, the event picks up and carries on. If something ends completely, that is not an intermission.

3. It is temporary.
An intermission always has a clear end. It lasts for a defined amount of time, and then normal proceedings resume. It is a gap, not a full stop.
Where You Will Most Commonly Encounter This Word

Theater and Stage Plays
This is the most classic and natural home of the word. A long stage play is often divided into two or more acts. The intermission falls between those acts — typically lasting around 15 to 20 minutes — giving the audience a chance to stand up, stretch, and breathe, and giving the crew backstage a chance to change the set.

"The first act ended on a cliffhanger, and the audience buzzed with excitement during the intermission."

Concerts and Musical Performances
A long orchestra concert, an opera, or a classical music performance often has an intermission between its two halves. Just like in theater, it gives musicians and audiences alike a moment of rest.

"During the intermission at the symphony, people streamed into the lobby to get a glass of wine."

Movies (Historically and Occasionally Today)
Decades ago, when films were exceptionally long — three, four, or even five hours — cinemas would build in an intermission so that audiences could use the restroom and buy refreshments. You do not see this very often today for regular films, but very long or epic films sometimes still include one.

"The nearly four-hour film featured an intermission halfway through, marked by a musical interlude on screen."

Formal Lectures, Seminars, and Conferences
Long lectures or all-day academic or professional events sometimes use the word intermission for a mid-session break, though the words "break" or "recess" are also common here.

Sports (Less Common)
In some sports contexts, you might encounter intermission used to describe the break between periods — particularly in ice hockey, where the break between the first and second periods, and between the second and third periods, is officially called an intermission.

"The coach addressed the team's weak defense during the intermission."
What People Do During an Intermission

Because an intermission is a designed break, it serves a social and practical purpose. People typically use the time to:

  • Visit the restroom
  • Buy refreshments (drinks, snacks)
  • Discuss what they have seen so far with friends
  • Simply rest and stretch after sitting for a long time

This is why intermissions in theaters and concert halls are almost always accompanied by an open lobby, a bar, or a refreshment counter — the whole experience is built around the pause.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are natural, varied examples to show you how the word works in real contexts:

  • "The ballet will have a twenty-minute intermission after the first act."
  • "I bumped into an old friend in the lobby during the intermission."
  • "Without an intermission, the three-hour play felt exhausting."
  • "The lights came up, signaling that intermission had begun."
  • "She stepped outside for some fresh air during the intermission."

Notice that "intermission" is often paired with words like during, after, before, at, and without.

Understanding a word fully means knowing how it differs from its close relatives.

Intermission vs. Break
"Break" is a much broader, everyday word. You take a break from work, from studying, from exercising. A "break" can be spontaneous, informal, and short. "Intermission," on the other hand, is more formal and is almost always tied to a structured public event like a performance. You would not say "I took an intermission from my homework." You would say you took a break.

Intermission vs. Interval
These two words are very close in meaning — nearly identical in many cases. Both refer to a pause in a performance. The key difference is geographical and stylistic: "interval" is the preferred term in British English, while "intermission" is standard in American English. If you are reading a British playbill, it will say "interval." An American one will say "intermission."

Intermission vs. Pause
A "pause" can be very brief — just a second or two — and it is a general word. An intermission is always a longer, more structured break with a clear social function attached to it.

Intermission vs. Recess
"Recess" is used specifically in formal or institutional settings: courts of law ("The court is in recess"), government legislatures, and schools ("children playing at recess"). Intermission belongs more naturally to the world of arts and entertainment.

Intermission vs. Halftime
"Halftime" is specific to sports and refers to the break in the exact middle of a game. It is a very particular kind of intermission. You could technically call halftime an intermission, but you would never call a theater's intermission a "halftime."

In more formal or literary writing, "intermission" can be used in a slightly broader sense to mean any temporary pause or break in a process — not necessarily a performance. For example:

"After working for hours without intermission, she finally stopped to eat."

Here, "without intermission" means without any pause at all — continuously, without stopping. This usage is less common in everyday speech but appears in older texts and formal writing. The core idea remains the same: a gap, a temporary halt in the middle of something ongoing.

To summarize everything: intermission means a planned, temporary break in the middle of a structured event or activity, after which the event continues. It is most at home in the world of theater, concerts, and formal performances. It is scheduled, purposeful, and has a social function. It is more formal than "break," more American than "interval," and more tied to performance than "recess." When you hear this word, picture the theater lights coming up, the curtain closed, and an audience flowing into a lobby — knowing the show is not over, just resting.

To intermit something means to stop it for a while, with the expectation — or implication — that it will start again.

It's not a permanent stop. It's a temporary pause, a break, a suspension. The thing that intermits goes away for a time, then comes back. That idea of coming back is absolutely central to this word.

Think of it like a traffic light. It doesn't stop forever — it stops, then goes, then stops again. That pattern of stopping-and-resuming is exactly the spirit of intermit.

The verb works in two ways:

1. You intermit something (transitive — you cause the pause):

You are actively making something stop for a while.

"The doctor advised her to intermit the medication for ten days."
(= stop taking it temporarily, then resume)

"He decided to intermit his exercise routine during the cold months."
(= pause it, not quit it forever)

2. Something intermits on its own (intransitive — it pauses by itself):

The thing itself stops and starts in a natural pattern, without you doing anything to it.

"The pain intermitted for several hours before returning."
(= it went away on its own for a while, then came back)

"The rain intermitted throughout the afternoon."
(= it kept stopping and starting)
The Key Feeling of the Word

The most important thing to understand is this: intermit carries a strong sense of rhythm or pattern. When something intermits, it usually doesn't just stop once and start once. It tends to stop, start, stop, start — repeatedly. This is why the adjective form, intermittent, describes things like an intermittent signal (one that keeps flickering on and off) or intermittent pain (pain that comes and goes).

So when you use intermit, you're almost always signaling that the stopping is part of a larger pattern, not a one-time thing.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where the word sharpens up significantly.

  • Stop / cease — These don't promise that the thing will return. "The music stopped" might mean it's over forever. "The music intermitted" tells you it will come back.
  • Pause — Very close in meaning, but pause is lighter and more conversational. It often describes a single, brief break. Intermit is more formal and often implies a longer break, or a recurring cycle of breaks.
  • Suspend — Suspend usually involves a deliberate decision by someone in authority. "The court suspended proceedings." Intermit can describe both deliberate pauses and natural, self-occurring ones. Also, suspend doesn't emphasize the coming-back as strongly.
  • Interrupt — Interrupt means something from outside cuts in and breaks the flow. Someone interrupts your speech. But intermit doesn't need an external cause — the thing itself can intermit naturally.
Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

Intermit is a formal word. You will encounter it most in:

  • Medical writing — Fevers, pulses, and symptoms intermit in classic medical descriptions.
  • Legal or official documents — Proceedings, duties, or obligations may be said to intermit.
  • Classic literature and philosophy — Older writers used it freely.
  • Formal academic prose — Especially in history, science, or theology.

You would almost never hear it in casual spoken conversation. In everyday speech, people would simply say "take a break from," "pause," or "stop for a while." But when precision and formality matter — and when you want to signal that the pause is part of a pattern rather than a permanent end — intermit is the exact right word.

"The committee chose to intermit the negotiations until a new proposal was ready."

"His enthusiasm for the project intermitted whenever the workload became too heavy, but always returned."

"The ancient custom had intermitted for decades before being revived in the 1980s."

"She had to intermit her studies for a semester due to illness."

Notice in each case: the stopping is temporary, the resumption is either stated or clearly implied.

To intermit is to stop something temporarily — especially in a recurring pattern — with the clear understanding that it will begin again.

If you grasp that: the stopping is not the end, it's just a break in an ongoing rhythm — you've understood intermit completely.

Intermittent means something that keeps stopping and starting again, rather than going on without any break.

If something is intermittent, it does not happen continuously. It happens for a while, then it stops, then it comes back again, then it stops again — and this cycle repeats. The essential idea is: gaps exist. There are interruptions in between.

Think of a dripping tap. It doesn't pour out water in a steady, unbroken stream. Instead: drip... silence... drip... silence... drip. That pattern — action, pause, action, pause — is what "intermittent" captures perfectly.

The simplest way to remember this word is to think of it as a more formal, precise way of saying "on and off."

  • Intermittent pain = pain that comes and goes, rather than hurting without stopping.
  • Intermittent rain = rain that falls for a while, stops, then falls again later.
  • Intermittent Wi-Fi = a connection that keeps dropping out and reconnecting.

In every case, the thing is present sometimes and absent other times. That back-and-forth is the heart of the word.

This is an important nuance. Intermittent can refer to either:

Regular pauses — where the stopping and starting happens on a predictable schedule. A lighthouse that flashes once every 8 seconds is intermittent in a perfectly regular way.

Irregular pauses — where the stopping and starting is unpredictable. A car alarm that randomly goes off and stops throughout the night is also intermittent.

The word works for both situations. It does not tell you how often the gaps occur or how long they last. It only tells you that the thing does not happen in one continuous, unbroken stretch. The gaps exist — but their timing and length are not specified by the word itself.

Weather: "There will be intermittent showers throughout the afternoon." This means it will rain for a bit, then stop, then rain again — not a steady downpour all day.

Health and medicine: "The patient experiences intermittent chest pain." The pain is not constant. It appears, disappears, and reappears at various times. (Doctors actually find intermittent symptoms trickier to diagnose than constant ones, for exactly this reason.)

Technology: "The printer has an intermittent fault." The printer doesn't fail every single time — it works sometimes and misbehaves at other times. This kind of problem is notoriously hard to fix because it doesn't happen reliably enough to pin down.

Electricity/Power: "The village suffered intermittent power cuts during the storm." The lights weren't out permanently — they kept going off and coming back on.

Sound: "She was distracted by the intermittent beeping from the next room." Not a constant beep, but one that kept occurring at intervals.

Diet and lifestyle: You may have heard the phrase "intermittent fasting." This is a way of eating where a person alternates between periods of eating and periods of fasting (not eating) — a perfect real-world use of the word.

It helps to be clear about what this word does not mean:

It does not mean something happening constantly or continuously. A river flowing without stopping is not intermittent — it is constant or continuous. A headache that has not stopped for three days straight is not intermittent — it is persistent or sustained.

It also does not mean something that happened only once. A single power cut that lasted two hours and never happened again is not intermittent — it is simply a one-time event. Intermittent implies repetition of that stopping-and-starting pattern.

Several words are close in meaning to intermittent, but each carries a slightly different shade:

Sporadic is very similar, but it tends to emphasize that the occurrences are rare and widely spaced out — almost scattered randomly. Intermittent simply means "with gaps"; sporadic suggests the gaps are quite long and the pattern is quite unpredictable. Sporadic violence in a region means it flares up very occasionally and randomly. Intermittent violence could mean it's happening more frequently, just not non-stop.

Periodic is also close, but it tilts in the opposite direction — toward regularity. Periodic suggests the gaps follow a predictable, almost clock-like schedule. Your heart beats periodically (at a regular rhythm). Intermittent does not require that kind of regularity.

Occasional focuses more on how rarely something happens, not on the stopping-and-starting pattern. An occasional cup of coffee means you don't drink it very often. Intermittent focuses on the pattern of gaps, not on the overall frequency.

On-and-off is the informal, everyday equivalent of intermittent. They mean the same thing. "They've had an on-and-off friendship for years" = "They've had an intermittent friendship for years." Intermittent simply sounds more formal and precise.

The clearest opposites of intermittent are:

  • Continuous — going on without any break at all.
  • Constant — happening all the time, without stopping.
  • Uninterrupted — not broken by any gaps or pauses.
  • Sustained — kept up steadily over a period of time without stopping.
  • Persistent — continuing to exist without going away.

If intermittent is the flickering candle, these words describe the steady, never-wavering flame.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Intermittent = stops and starts, repeatedly, with gaps in between.

It is not constant, not one-time, and not necessarily regular or irregular — just not continuous. Whether it's rain, pain, a signal, a sound, or a problem, if it keeps coming and going rather than persisting without a break, the right word for it is intermittent.
